title: Defense in Depth, Rebuilt for Machine Speed | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z argues AI has made exploits cheap (hours) while patching still takes weeks to years (Verizon 2026: 43-day median remediation; Veracode: 252 days), so the exploit-patch gap will not close and value shifts to controls that work without patches: removing exposure, segmentation, AI-generated virtual patching, bug-class elimination and proven recovery. It maps six merged-category startup opportunities, from 'fix it live, then fix the code' and rule-less AI SOCs to per-request agent identity, backup posture management, install-point supply-chain gateways and a long-tail OT platform.

insights.claim: AI made turning a bug into a working exploit cheap in 2025-2026 while patching did not get faster, so the exploit-to-patch gap will not close by patching harder; the products and policies that matter over the next five years protect systems that cannot be patched quickly.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Security spend shifts from patch velocity toward compensating controls that work without patches.
insights.quote: Our view is that the gap between exploit and patch won’t close by patching harder
insights.locator: In our last piece, we argued

insights.claim: Patch remediation remains slow and is getting slower: the 2026 Verizon breach report put median full remediation at 43 days with only 26% of known-exploited vulnerabilities fully remediated, and Veracode's 2025 report put average flaw-remediation time at 252 days, up from 171 five years earlier.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Defender cycle times are measured in weeks to months versus attacker cycle times in hours.
insights.quote: Veracode’s 2025 report put average flaw-remediation time at 252 days, up from 171 five years earlier.
insights.locator: The arithmetic doesn’t close

insights.claim: In October 2026 Anthropic reported an unreleased model produced a remote, no-login exploit for a Linux kernel bug fixed upstream weeks earlier, winning in under an hour a timing race Red Hat had rated only moderate because it was hard to win; two widely used server distributions still had no fixed package.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Severity ratings based on exploit difficulty are obsolete when AI can win hard races quickly.
insights.quote: Red Hat had rated the bug moderate because its timing race was hard to win. The model won it in under an hour.
insights.locator: Discovery is moving differently.

insights.claim: Speeding up patch deployment is itself risky: one faulty CrowdStrike update in July 2024 crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines, and deploying patches hundreds or thousands of times a day would swap attacks for self-inflicted downtime.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Faster patching is not a free fix; the goal becomes needing to patch less.
insights.quote: if patches need to be deployed 100s or 1000s of times a day, you just swap attacks for self-inflicted downtime.
insights.locator: Even where patching can speed up

insights.claim: In October two critical PHP bugs leaked before their fix with exploit attempts starting four days before disclosure; hosting and CDN companies blocked attacks at the edge, but 2.6 to 4.4 million PHP installations outside that umbrella stayed exposed, most on versions that will never be fixed.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Edge-provider shielding can protect without patches, but only for those behind the platform.
insights.quote: between 2.6 and 4.4 million PHP installations outside that umbrella stayed exposed, most of them on versions that will never get a fix.
insights.locator: In October, two critical bugs

themes.theme: Systems that will never be patched in time

insights.claim: Industrial control systems are patched in maintenance windows, often annually; Dragos found about a quarter of 2025's industrial advisories shipped with no patch or mitigation at all, and US grid rules allow 35 days to evaluate a patch plus 35 more to apply it.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: OT/grid/water security must rely on off-device controls rather than vendor patches.
insights.quote: Dragos found that about a quarter of 2025’s industrial advisories shipped with no patch or mitigation at all
insights.locator: Industrial control systems.

insights.claim: Medical devices such as infusion pumps, imaging systems and ECMO machines live 10-20 years often on unsupported operating systems, FDA cybersecurity rules apply only to new devices, and a 2025 survey found 89% of hospital systems had connected devices with a known-exploited vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Hospital device fleets are a large unpatchable attack surface needing network-level protection.
insights.quote: In one 2025 survey, 89% of hospital systems had connected devices with a known-exploited vulnerability.
insights.locator: Medical devices.

insights.claim: In October attackers heated refrigeration in hundreds of French supermarkets in one night via end-of-life controllers; the national cyber agency's only advice was to disconnect, the attack spread three weeks later to Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden and Estonia, and one contractor said the fix needs physical changes to every unit.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Unowned, unpatchable connected devices create real physical and economic losses across borders.
insights.quote: attackers heated the refrigeration in hundreds of French supermarkets in one night, mostly through end-of-life controllers that no longer get fixes.
insights.locator: Everything else with a chip.

insights.claim: For long-lived and slow-update equipment, patching was never really the security control but a hope; the controls that actually work sit off the device.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Invest in network, access and recovery layers rather than device-level remediation for OT and IoT.
insights.quote: For all of these, patching was never really the control. It was the hope. The controls that work are off the device.
insights.locator: For all of these, patching was

themes.theme: Four scalable defenses ranked by reach

insights.claim: Removing systems from the open internet is the highest-reach defense: after Censys found nearly 400 exposed water-utility control screens (40 controllable without login) and worked with the EPA and vendor, a quarter were secured in nine days and fewer than 6% remained exposed by May 2025, with no patch involved.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Exposure reduction outpaces any patch cycle when routed through parties owners answer to.
insights.quote: No patch was involved, and it moved faster than any patch cycle could.
insights.locator: 1. Get it off the open internet.

insights.claim: Who delivers the remediation message matters: a European ISP's quarantine-and-notification process cleared 92% of infected consumer devices within 14 days, while email warnings did no better than nothing; AI makes finding exposure nearly free but getting owners to act is the hard part.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Distribution through ISPs, vendors, regulators or insurers is the bottleneck and the moat for exposure-management products.
insights.quote: Email warnings did no better than saying nothing.
insights.locator: Who delivers the message matters.

insights.claim: Network segmentation stopped an AI-driven intrusion: Dragos documented an intruder using a frontier model as its main operator reach the boundary between a Mexican water utility's office network and its control system and stop there because the control network was walled off.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Old, unglamorous segmentation keeps network intrusions from becoming physical events, even against AI attackers.
insights.quote: Segmentation is old and unglamorous, but it can keep a network intrusion from becoming a physical event.
insights.locator: 2. Segment what has to stay connected.

insights.claim: Virtual patching, historically a web-traffic product for big platforms, should evolve to generate protective rules automatically from each disclosure using the same AI that writes exploits and push them to industrial protocols, hospital networks and small-business routers.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Automated virtual patching for non-web and long-tail networks is a product opportunity.
insights.quote: The next step is to generate those rules automatically from each disclosure, using the same AI that writes the exploits
insights.locator: 3. Block the attack in the network

insights.claim: Eliminating bug classes is the only approach that shrinks the number of bugs to find: Google reports memory-safety bugs fell from 76% of Android's vulnerabilities in 2019 to 24% in 2024, mostly by writing new code in memory-safe languages.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Memory-safe migration is slow but the only durable reduction in vulnerability supply.
insights.quote: memory-safety bugs fell from 76% of Android’s vulnerabilities in 2019 to 24% in 2024
insights.locator: 4. Remove the whole class.

insights.claim: Alongside the four defenses, organizations need safe manual fallback (a water plant operable by hand, a hospital able to run on paper for a week) and must retire devices too old to protect economically.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Resilience planning must include manual operations and hardware retirement budgets.
insights.quote: A water plant needs to be able to operate by hand, a hospital needs to be able to work on paper for a week.
insights.locator: Two more investments belong alongside

themes.theme: Backups are attack surface, not insurance

insights.claim: Ransomware groups now target backups as a primary objective: in Sophos's 2024 survey 94% of ransomware victims said attackers tried to compromise backups and 57% of those attempts succeeded; Mandiant describes groups hitting backup infrastructure, identity and hypervisor management together.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Backup systems need the same hardening as production, including isolated credentials.
insights.quote: 94% said attackers had tried to compromise their backups, and 57% of those attempts succeeded.
insights.locator: Backups are now a primary target.

insights.claim: Recovery confidence far exceeds reality: in Veeam's 2026 survey 90% of leaders said they could meet recovery targets but only 28% of victims got all data back, and healthcare use of backups to recover encrypted data fell to 51% in 2025 from 72% three years earlier.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Untested recovery assumptions are a hidden enterprise risk and a sales wedge for verification products.
insights.quote: 90% of leaders said they could meet their recovery targets, but only 28% of victims got all their data back.
insights.locator: Confidence has not caught up.

insights.claim: Compromised backups raise median ransomware recovery costs to about $3 million versus $375,000 when backups survive; intact-backup victims were also more likely to be fully back within a week (46% vs 26%) and about half as likely to pay a ransom.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Backup integrity is roughly an 8x swing in incident cost.
insights.quote: median recovery costs of about $3 million, against $375,000 where the backups survived.
insights.locator: Confidence has not caught up.

insights.claim: A credible recovery posture is a proven, timed restore, not the existence of backups; backups need protected credentials, immutable copies, isolation from attacker access paths and regular restoration tests.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Boards and insurers should demand restore evidence rather than backup attestations.
insights.quote: “We have backups” is not a posture.
insights.locator: The lesson is that backups are

insights.claim: Protection is concentrating in a few cloud, content and security firms: the largest CDN now sits in front of a quarter of all websites, up from under 4% a decade ago, which is why the PHP response worked but also creates a single point of failure.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Platform concentration is both the defense mechanism and a systemic risk.
insights.quote: The largest content-delivery network alone now sits in front of a quarter of all websites, up from under 4% a decade ago.
insights.locator: The umbrella has a shape, and a cost

insights.claim: The July 2024 CrowdStrike outage cost the largest US companies an estimated $5.4 billion, with insurance expected to cover only 10 to 20%, illustrating correlated single-vendor risk.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Correlated vendor failures are largely uninsured losses.
insights.quote: it cost the largest US companies an estimated $5.4 billion, of which insurance was expected to cover only 10 to 20%
insights.locator: The umbrella has a shape, and a cost

insights.claim: Reliance on a handful of US platforms to decide which traffic reaches the world's servers raises a sovereignty question regulators are only starting to ask, as Jason Healey has noted.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Expect non-US regulatory pushback on US-platform-mediated internet security.
insights.quote: whose rules apply when a handful of US platforms decide which traffic reaches the world’s servers?
insights.locator: The umbrella has a shape, and a cost

insights.claim: Because defending a single asset costs about the same while attacking keeps getting cheaper, the long tail must either shelter under someone's platform or get exposed infrastructure off the internet; county water systems, clinics and small manufacturers doing neither are already paying.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Economics push small operators toward managed platforms, consolidating the security market.
insights.quote: Defending a single asset costs about what it always did, while attacking it keeps getting cheaper.
insights.locator: The economics push in one direction

insights.claim: Courts have already authorized the FBI to fix private machines without owner action: removing web shells from hundreds of Exchange servers in April 2021 and removing a Chinese state botnet from hundreds of mostly unsupported small-office routers in December 2023.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Legal precedent exists for state remediation of privately owned devices.
insights.quote: a US court authorized the FBI to remove malicious web shells from hundreds of private Exchange servers whose owners hadn’t acted.
insights.locator: There is precedent.

insights.claim: Pressure will grow for broader state intervention escalating from notify to quarantine to remediate devices that endanger others, a real civil-liberties trade-off better argued now than improvised in a crisis.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Policy debate on mandated device quarantine/remediation is coming.
insights.quote: Pressure for broader intervention will grow: notify, then quarantine, then remediate devices that endanger others.
insights.locator: There is precedent.

insights.claim: Winning security categories make patching unnecessary or someone else's job and merge multiple legacy categories; standalone old categories risk becoming features, and the company that takes the merged category starting from its hardest part has a shot at being generational.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Investors should favor platforms that collapse find-protect-verify into one product.
insights.quote: The old categories on their own are at risk of becoming a feature in this new world.
insights.locator: The old categories on their own

insights.claim: Pentesting, vulnerability management and application security merge into a 'fix it live, then fix the code' loop: mitigate in the running system within hours via edge rules, in-process hooks or in-memory patches, while coding agents write version-specific code fixes and retire the live fix once shipped.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Production, not source code, becomes the first place security fixes land.
insights.quote: Fix it live in hours, fix the code in days.
insights.locator: 1. Fix it live, then fix the code.

insights.claim: Europe's Cyber Resilience Act requires covered manufacturers since September 2026 to issue an early warning within 24 hours of learning a vulnerability is exploited, and from December 2027 to handle vulnerabilities throughout each product's support period, pressuring vendors toward fast backporting.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Regulation creates a paying vendor-side market for automated fix and backport tooling.
insights.quote: covered manufacturers have had to issue an early warning within 24 hours of learning that a vulnerability is being exploited
insights.locator: The same machinery belongs on the vendor side

insights.claim: Runtime exploit prevention scales better than chasing bugs because exploitation techniques are few: of 48,185 vulnerabilities published in 2025 only 884 were newly exploited, and CISA found most weakness types behind exploited bugs are ones the industry has known how to prevent for decades.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Technique-level runtime defenses with small inline models offer leverage over per-CVE work.
insights.quote: Of the 48,185 vulnerabilities published in 2025, 884 were newly exploited
insights.locator: Writing exploits is becoming cheaper

insights.claim: Rule-based detection is breaking down: Vectra's 2026 survey found teams see about 3,000 alerts a day and never get to 63%, 40% had switched off or considered switching off a rule, and 60% had seen an uninvestigated alert become a real incident.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Supports an AI SOC that merges detection, managed detection and incident response into a first-responder service.
insights.quote: security teams saw about 3,000 alerts a day and never got to 63% of them.
insights.locator: Detection today runs on rules

insights.claim: The winning AI SOC reads events directly from existing security products rather than after SIEM ingestion, since cost pressure leads teams to drop evidence, and it acts as first responder with humans approving only production-impacting actions.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: SIEM-centric architectures face disintermediation by source-reading AI responders.
insights.quote: An intruder who got in at machine speed moves at machine speed, so the response has to as well.
insights.locator: That makes it the first responder

insights.claim: AI agents broke the assumption that a user and a machine are the same principal; identity, endpoint and network access must merge into per-request trust decisions made on the endpoint, with just-in-time credentials scoped to one task and lasting minutes.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Agent proliferation drives demand for endpoint-attributed, per-request access control.
insights.quote: Trust has to be judged per request, by who or what produced it
insights.locator: 3. Judge every request, not every login.

insights.claim: Backup, disaster recovery and cyber insurance merge into 'backup posture management' that continuously restores real systems into a clean room and produces evidence insurers accept; this record becomes the underwriting input for correlated losses insurers currently exclude.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Proven-recovery data could unlock underwriting of correlated cyber risk.
insights.quote: Correlated losses, where one shared bug hits thousands of victims at once, are difficult to model and price and exactly what insurers exclude today.
insights.locator: The recovery record is also the underwriting input.

insights.claim: Many large losses start with no bug to patch: Binance puts an October theft at $6.3 billion tied to one engineer's compromised laptop, and Verizon found phishing, stolen credentials and pretexting at 35% of initial access versus 31% for exploited bugs, with third parties in 48% of breaches, up from 15% two years earlier.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Supply-chain and developer-endpoint controls modeled on email gateways are a growing market.
insights.quote: A third party was involved in 48% of breaches, up from 15% two years earlier.
insights.locator: In Verizon’s latest report

insights.claim: Supply-chain security should copy the email-gateway model applied to package managers, extension marketplaces, vendor connections and AI agent skills: hold, detonate in a sandbox and verify provenance under one policy, because for an agent a document is also an instruction.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Agent tool and skill ingestion is a new channel requiring gateway-style screening.
insights.quote: For an agent a document is also an instruction.
insights.locator: The model is the one email security

insights.claim: A long-tail platform combining exposure management, secure remote access, control-network segmentation and manual fallback can serve water utilities, hospital biomedical departments and refrigeration contractors that will never run a security team, sold through vendors, ISPs or insurers.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Managed-service model for non-cloud OT is an underserved opportunity.
insights.quote: Exposure removal only works as a product if it sells the alternative
insights.locator: 6. The long-tail platform.

insights.claim: AI translation makes migrating to memory-safe code newly practical, though it reaches the long tail last.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: AI-assisted memory-safe rewrites could accelerate bug-class elimination.
insights.quote: migrating to memory-safe code is newly practical because AI can do much of the translation.
insights.locator: Alongside these products, migrating

insights.claim: 2026 looks less like the start of a cyber war than the start of a long, expensive worm era; unlike the last worm era, which ended when one company took ownership of the problem, nobody owns this one, so the exploit-patch window will stay open for many systems.
insights.speaker: Asaf Ezra, Stephenie Zhang
insights.so_what: Plan for chronic, distributed cyber losses rather than a single resolving event.
insights.quote: The last worm era ended when one company took ownership of the problem and fixed it. Nobody owns this one.
insights.locator: The last piece ended with a wager
